lines.text: Your phone battery lasted all day when it was new. Now it's dead by lunch. What actually happened inside?
Inside are two layers. On one side, layers of graphite. On the other, a metal oxide. Between them, a liquid.
When you charge, lithium ions are pushed across, and packed into the graphite, like cars into a parking garage.
When you use your phone, they flow back. And for every ion that crosses inside, an electron runs through your phone outside. That's the power.
But every trip leaves a little damage. A crusty film grows on the graphite, and it traps some lithium for good.
Fewer ions left to travel means less charge. After a few hundred full cycles, many batteries are down to about eighty percent.
Heat makes it worse. So does sitting at a hundred percent for hours, or draining all the way to zero.
That's why phones now offer to stop charging at eighty percent. It keeps the garage from being packed too tight.
And to send a big file, you don't need another app draining your phone. Orbi Transfer is just a website. No install, no login.
